title: Conway's Law and Why Architecture Mirrors Org Structure (1967)
explainer: Melvin Conway argued in his 1967/68 article 'How Do Committees Invent?' that any organization designing a system tends to produce a design that mirrors its own communication structure. For AI-powered systems, where a single user-facing feature often hides separate teams for data pipelines, model serving, retrieval, and safety guardrails, this is a genuine warning: the seams in your architecture, and many of your integration bugs, often trace back to team boundaries rather than technical necessity. It's a real lens for deciding where to draw service boundaries when architecting an AI system end to end.

title: Brewer's CAP Theorem and the Limits of Distributed Architecture (2000)
explainer: Eric Brewer conjectured in 2000, and Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch formally proved in 2002, that a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance - at most two of the three hold at once during a network partition. AI-powered systems that spread model serving, vector databases, and feature stores across multiple nodes inherit this constraint directly: choosing a vector store or a caching layer is really choosing which of C, A, or P you're willing to sacrifice. It turns an architecture 'tradeoff' into a named, provable limit rather than a vague engineering intuition.
